The market at {x} is audible before it is visible: a specific mix of voices, animals, and the percussion of commerce that no other combination of sounds quite replicates.
{x}'s market day has the comfortable chaos of something that has been happening in the same place for a long time and has worked out most of its problems.
The road into {x} is thick with carts by mid-morning, all of them heading for the same square, and the traffic tells you where the settlement's heart is before you can see it.
You reach {x} against a tide of people leaving it. The market has ended for the day, and the settlement is exhaling its visitors back onto the roads with their purchases and their news.
The smell of the river reaches you before the settlement does: clean water, reeds, the particular mud of a working waterfront.
{x} runs along the water the way settlements do when water is the reason they exist: practical, a little chaotic at the waterfront, tidier as you move inland.
The river carries the sounds of {x} to you around the bend before the buildings appear: a mill wheel, the knock of boats against a jetty, someone calling a tally across the water.

{x} has its back to the land and its face to the river; the approach by road brings you in the rear way, past the yards and the drying nets, into a settlement that plainly considers the water its front door.
The harbour at {x} announces itself beyond the last rise: masts above the roofs, gulls wheeling over the quays, and salt bright in the air.
{x} faces the sea as deliberately as a fortress faces its enemy. Warehouses and chandlers crowd the waterfront, with the older streets climbing behind them.
You hear {x}'s harbour before you see it: rigging knocking against masts, dock crews calling cargo tallies, and surf working against the outer wall.
The road into {x} descends toward a forest of masts. Tar, salt, fish, and woodsmoke mark the boundary between the coast and the working port.
The cookfire smoke of {x} drifts on the wind in your direction: a hundred fires, each with its own particular fuel, combining into something that smells like inhabited place.
{x} is visible as a smear of smoke on the horizon for a long time before the buildings resolve.
You smell {x} before anything else: woodsmoke and bread and livestock, the layered scent of a place where people have been living close together and cooking the same suppers for generations.
The smoke above {x} stands straight up in the still air, a dozen thin columns that mark the settlement's shape on the sky like a map drawn in grey.
The sound of a hammer on metal reaches you from {x}'s smithing quarter: a craftsperson's rhythm, not a soldier's.
{x} smells of work: sawdust, tallow, the particular sharp smell of a tanner at the edge of town.
{x} announces its trade before its name: the whine of a lathe, the reek of the dye-vats, a workshop door standing open on a scene of unhurried, practised industry.
The approach to {x} is lined with the overflow of its crafts: timber stacked to season, half-finished goods under eaves, the settlement's work spilling out past its walls for want of room inside.
{x} is ordinary in the best sense: a place where people live and work and argue and sleep, which is most of what places are for.
The road into {x} becomes a street at a point you can't precisely identify. The settlement grows around you gradually.
{x} is neither impressive nor disappointing from the approach. It is what it is, which is a working settlement of reasonable size doing reasonable things.
A child runs past you on the road into {x}, chasing something or being chased by something (unclear which). Nobody in the street pays attention.
A merchant argues with a carter at the gate of {x} about the size of a load. The guard is ignoring both of them. This is clearly a daily occurrence.
{x} smells like bread from the gate: a bakehouse near the entrance, open early, already on the second bake of the day.
The {x} of {x} announces itself before the settlement does: masts above the treeline, the smell of tar and salt, the cries of gulls working the fishing boats.
{x} appears as a smear of colour above the water: pennants, sail canvas, the white of new-washed walls catching the light from the sea.
The approach to {x} is along the quayside road, which means threading through loaded carts and dock workers before the settlement itself comes into view.
You smell {x} before you see it: smoke, fish, the mineral bite of the harbour at low tide.
{x} sits in the bend of the river, its rooftops visible above the willows from a quarter mile out. The mill wheel turns.
The river road into {x} runs alongside the water, and the settlement grows out of the bank on both sides: older buildings on the high ground, newer ones crowding the waterfront.
You cross the river at the ford half a mile out and the road becomes a proper street almost immediately. {x} has been expanding toward the water.
The bridge into {x} is old stone, wide enough for two carts, and there is already a queue to cross it.
{x} is visible from the junction itself. The roads converge on a market square that seems to be the settlement's reason for existing.
Four roads, and {x} at the centre of all of them. Travellers in three directions. The fourth road is yours.
The waymarker stone at the crossroads half a league out has {x}'s name carved into it four times, facing each direction. Someone keeps repainting the distances.
{x} sprawls along all four roads from the central square. The part you see first depends on which direction you came from.
{x} appears around a bend in the road, its {x} coming into view all at once.
The road widens into {x}'s main thoroughfare without announcing the transition. You are in the settlement before you realised you arrived.
A mile marker, then a second, then the outlying farms of {x} begin. The settlement proper is still a quarter hour ahead.
{x} is announced by the smoke of its cookfires and the sound of its market before its buildings are visible.
{x} appears at the end of a track that stopped pretending to be a road some time ago. It exists here because someone decided to stay, not because the terrain made it easy.
The last real road ended two hours back. {x} is visible now: a cluster of buildings in the middle distance that the surrounding terrain seems indifferent to.
The track into {x} is maintained by the people who need it, which means it is exactly wide enough and no wider.
{x} sits in a natural fold of the terrain, protected on three sides. You see the smoke before the buildings, and the buildings before you find the path down.

The gates of {x} are closed. There are people on the walls. This is not the relaxed watch of a settlement going about its day. These are people watching the treeline. A runner comes out of the small side gate, sees your group, stops.

{x}'s gates are open but attended: every person entering is noted, every cart searched. The guards are professional about it, which makes it worse. Professional means this has been happening long enough to become routine.

From the road, {x} looks ordinary. Smoke from cookfires, the sound of a market. It is only at the gate that the weight becomes apparent: the guards' expressions, the way conversation stops when strangers approach.

The approach to {x} is quieter than it should be for a settlement this size. The outlying farms are empty. The road has not been maintained recently. The settlement itself is intact, but everything around it has been abandoned to the walls.
The fields around {x} were harvested early and badly: stubble cut in haste, carts gone. Whatever the walls are waiting for, the granaries inside are already keeping its schedule.
A thrown stone sits half-buried a hundred paces short of {x}'s wall, left where it landed. Nobody has hauled it away. There are fresher things to attend to.

{x} looks prosperous in the merchant quarter: new paint, loaded carts, a market stall with produce. It is only when you walk further in that the other version of the settlement appears: shuttered houses, people sitting on doorsteps with no particular purpose.
{x} is functional. The market is open, the streets are swept, the guards are at their posts. Something is wrong anyway. It takes a moment to identify: there are no children playing in the street.

The queue at the granary gate is the first thing you see in {x}. Not a market queue, not a water queue: the organised, patient, daily queue of people who are waiting to receive what they are owed and are not certain they will receive it.

{x} is orderly in the way that a settlement is orderly when order is being enforced. The streets are clear. The rationing markers are painted on the doors. A guard patrol passes and everyone steps aside.
The dogs of {x} are gone. It takes a while to notice and longer to stop noticing, and nobody in the settlement will discuss it with a stranger.

Prices chalked outside {x}'s market gate have been rubbed out and rewritten so often the board has gone grey. The numbers on it now are polite fictions; the real trading happens in back rooms, in kind.

The flags above {x}'s gatehouse are not the settlement's own. Two soldiers at the gate. Their uniform is not local. They look at your papers with the particular expression of people who have been told to look at papers.

{x} looks normal from the approach. It is only at the gate that the nature of normal becomes apparent: the guard asks where you are from, writes it down, and asks how long you intend to stay. This is not the usual question.
The approach to {x} looks like any other settlement. There is graffiti on the wall near the gate that someone has attempted to scrub off. The symbol is still readable.

{x} is going about its business. The market is open, the streets are busy, the gates are attended by soldiers whose armour is not local. Everyone is doing what they are supposed to be doing, which is the point.
{x}'s street signs have been repainted in two languages, the local one second. The new lettering is neat, official, and everywhere, which is how you learn the occupation intends to stay.
At {x}'s gate the queue divides in two: residents with papers, and everyone else. The residents' line is longer and moves slower, and no one in it complains where the soldiers can hear.
{x} has two gates. The eastern one is controlled by one faction, the western by another. You can tell by the pennants. The road you are on leads to the eastern gate.
The gate guard at {x} asks where you intend to stay: which inn, which district. The answer apparently matters. They note it and say nothing further.

The road into {x} has been marked. Symbols painted on fence posts and milestone stones: the same symbol, repeated, belonging to one faction or another. Someone has been doing this recently; the paint is fresh.

{x} is quieter than it should be. Not the quiet of a sleeping town or a working one: the particular quiet of a place where people have learned to be careful about what they say in earshot of strangers.

Two tax collectors work {x}'s market: different sashes, different ledgers, studiously ignoring one another. Traders pay one, or the other, or both, according to calculations a visitor is not equipped to make.
The council hall of {x} is dark; the business of governing has moved to two different taverns at opposite ends of town. Which one you drink in has become a declaration.

{x} is in reasonable shape. The walls are standing, the market is functioning, the main street is paved. The paving needs repair. The wall has a section of new brick that doesn't quite match the old. The repairs that needed doing five years ago are still waiting.

A building near the gate has a new sign: an institution that wasn't there last season, with a name that is recognisably the name of an outside creditor. Someone has arrived and set up an office. This is not a good sign.
{x} functions. The market is busy enough. The streets are clean enough. The civic buildings are maintained enough. 'Enough' is doing a lot of work in every impression.
The merchant district of {x} looks prosperous. The rest of the settlement, visible further in, looks like it has been waiting for the merchant district's prosperity to reach it for some years.

The finest building in {x} is new, stone-built, and belongs to nobody local: a counting house, its brass plate polished daily by a clerk who arrived with the ledgers. It is what everything else in town is working to pay for.

{x} holds a market day that has quietly become a collection day: the stalls pay their pitch fees to a factor before they sell a thing, and the factor's book has more names in it than the market has stalls.
The guard at {x}'s gate is polite, thorough, and writes down more than guards usually write down. You are asked your business three times, by three different people, in the space of five minutes.

Something happened in {x} recently. You cannot immediately say what, but the settlement has the quality of a place that is still processing something: hushed conversations, people watching the street.

There are notices posted at the gate of {x}. You take a moment to read one: it is asking for information about a specific event, with a contact at the council offices. The date on the notice is recent.
{x} looks ordinary from the approach. It is only in the expressions of the people at the gate (watchful in a specific, tired way) that something registers.
{x} has new locks. You can see the bright hasps on doors and shutters as you walk in: ironmongery bought all at once, recently, by people who used not to need it.

Conversation in {x}'s common room stops at the creak of the door-hinge, resumes a beat later, carefully general. Whatever happened here, everyone has already said everything they intend to say about it.
{x} looks exactly like it should. The gate is attended, the market sounds busy, there is nothing remarkable about the approach. Everything is as it should be.
The approach to {x} is unremarkable in every respect. Gate, road, market noise, smoke, the usual questions from the guard. Nothing to note.
{x} looks normal. There is a moment at the gate (a guard glancing at another guard after you answer a question) that is probably nothing.
{x} is functioning well. Clean streets, busy market, maintained walls. If you were looking for problems, you would not find them from the outside.
Nothing in {x} is out of place. The watch changes on the hour, the market closes at dusk, the innkeeper remembers your name on the second morning. It is all exactly as a well-run town should be.
{x} welcomes travellers with practised ease: a good inn, fair prices, incurious guards. A week later you would struggle to say why the ease sat strangely. It was practised.

The approach to {x} is interrupted by a checkpoint a quarter mile from the gates: a temporary structure, manned by people wearing cloth over their faces. They want to know where you came from and when.

{x}'s gate is open, the market is running, and there are people in the street. People are giving each other slightly more space than usual. A cart passes with barrels marked with an unfamiliar symbol. You have seen that symbol once before, on a quarantine notice.
Near the gate of {x} there is a temporary shelter: a healer's station, by the look of it, with two attendants and a queue. The queue is not yet long. That is either good or early.

Some of {x}'s market stalls are closed. Not all, not most, but several, in a pattern that isn't about the day of the week. The ones that are open are busy; the ones that are closed have been for a while.
{x}'s gate stands open, but the gatekeeper waves you through from a distance, and the well just inside has been roped off under a painted sign too weathered to read from horseback.
Smoke rises from {x} at midday: not cookfires but something being burned deliberately, bedding or clothes, in a yard behind the healer's house. The street watches it burn and says nothing.
There are two sets of pennants above {x}'s main gate: different colours, same height. Someone made a decision to hang them both and has committed to maintaining the ambiguity.
{x} has the specific quality of a settlement waiting for news. People are going about their business, but there is a particular alertness to the street: people checking who is talking to whom.

The road into {x} has been busy recently. You can tell by the wheel ruts, the quality of the mud, the number of horses at the inn you pass on the approach. Something is happening that requires people to arrive quickly.
{x} functions, after a fashion. The market is open, the gates are attended. The flagpole above the council building is empty. Someone removed the standard and hasn't replaced it yet.
The masons of {x} have stopped mid-job on the great house; scaffolding stands empty on dressed stone. Work that fine waits on a patron, and the town is not currently sure who that is.
In {x}'s taproom the toast is to "the settlement": a formulation everyone has adopted at once, smooth as furniture, since naming anyone more specific has become a wager.
{x} is more fortified than its size suggests. The walls are new (or newly repaired), the mortar still pale. There are more torches at the gate than a settlement like this would normally need.

The farms outside {x} are partially abandoned. You count three sets of buildings that have not been worked recently: the fields untended, the doors standing open. The settlement's wall is a quarter mile closer than it would have been three months ago.
{x}'s gate is attended by its usual guards and, less usually, by several people in road-worn equipment who are clearly not local and clearly not merchants. The settlement is paying for help.

{x} is going about its business, but the business includes people you wouldn't normally see on a market day: hunters checking arrows, a blacksmith working past dark, a group of militia running a drill in the square visible from the gate.
The road into {x} runs its last mile between new watchtowers: timber, hasty, manned. Whatever they watch for, the fields between them have been let go to seed.
{x} buys arrows. The fletcher's is the busiest shop in the settlement, and the militia board outside the gate lists a standing bounty in terms that carefully avoid naming what it is for.

The approach to {x} is ordinary until you notice what is missing: no toll-keeper at the gate, no one collecting the road tax a settlement this size always collects. The guards are present, but they are watching the town, not the road.

{x}'s gate stands open and unmanned. Further in, two different sets of notices are posted on the same wall: one in the formal hand of the authorities, one hand-lettered and torn at the corner. Someone tears down the second kind. Someone keeps putting them back.

There are soldiers on {x}'s streets, but they move in pairs and do not linger. The people watch them pass with the particular blankness of a place that has already decided which side it is on and is waiting to be asked.

{x} looks governed, and is not, quite. The market runs, the watch patrols, the council building is occupied. But the orders that leave that building are not always the orders that get followed, and everyone in the street knows which is which.
The garrison of {x} patrols in daylight only, and along routes a stranger could predict by the third day. After dark the town belongs to whoever it belongs to.
Someone has been chalking a sign on {x}'s walls faster than the watch can scrub it. By now the scrubbed patches themselves mark every corner. The censorship has become the graffiti.

The road into {x} is crowded: not with merchants but with families, carts piled with household goods, people who are clearly not from here and clearly not passing through. The gate guard has stopped checking papers. There are too many.

{x} has grown a second settlement outside its walls: tents and lean-tos and cookfires on the ground that used to be common pasture. The people there watch you approach with the wariness of those who arrived too late to get inside.

Half of {x} seems to be leaving. You pass loaded wagons heading the other way on the road, and inside the walls there are shuttered houses and shops with their goods already gone. Those who remain have the look of people deciding whether to be next.

{x}'s market speaks three languages you can pick out and more you cannot. The old families and the newcomers trade at the same stalls and do not quite look at each other. Everyone is doing business. No one is comfortable.
The road to {x} has acquired a verge of graves: recent, orderly, unmarked but tended. People arrived here in numbers, and not all of them finished the journey.
{x}'s smithy has a queue for wheel-rims and none for ploughshares. A town where the carts outnumber the fields is a town in the middle of someone's arithmetic about leaving.

The road to {x} has been rutted deep by heavy wagons moving in one direction: toward the settlement loaded, away from it loaded differently. At the gate a clerk in crown colours records what comes and goes. This is not a market town's traffic.

{x}'s young men are not in {x}. You notice it at the gate and it holds true inside: the people working the stalls and the fields are the old, the very young, and the women. A recruiting notice is nailed to the gatepost, its edges soft with weather.

There are more soldiers than citizens visible on {x}'s main street, and the citizens are the ones stepping aside. A requisition column is being loaded in the square: grain, cloth, iron, and the settlement's own carts to carry it away.

{x} is prosperous in a way that feels wrong. The forges work past dark, the warehouses are full, the coin is moving, and all of it points one direction, toward a war that is not fought here but is paid for here.
{x}'s noticeboard is a wall of requisition orders, each stamped, each superseding the last. At its foot, a smaller paper, hand-lettered: prayers offered nightly, all welcome.
The horses in {x}'s paddocks are old, or lame, or foals. Every sound animal of working age has a receipt where it used to be, and the receipts do not say when the crown returns them.

Two temples face each other across {x}'s central square, and only one has a queue. The other's doors are open but its steps are swept too clean, walked on too little. Something has moved from one building to the other, and it was not only worshippers.

The shrine at {x}'s gate has been recently altered: one symbol chiselled away, another set in its place, the old outline still faintly visible beneath the new. Someone did this carefully. Someone else has been scratching at the replacement.

{x} is observing a holy day, and you cannot tell which one. Some shops are shut and draped; others are pointedly open. Two processions are forming in different quarters, and the people watching each are counting who watches the other.

The bells of {x} ring at competing times: one set of chimes answered a beat later by another, from a different quarter, slightly out of tune with the first. No one seems to find this strange, which is the strangest part.
The mason's yard in {x} is its busiest enterprise: one set of holy symbols coming down, another going up, and the same three workmen paid for both. They no longer joke about it.
{x} has two burial grounds now, one old and one new, and the town's grief is learning to sort itself accordingly. The gravedigger serves both and is the most carefully neutral man alive.

{x}'s gates are shut in daylight, which is wrong for a settlement of its size. There is smoke inside: not cookfire smoke, too much and too dark. On the wall, the guards face inward, toward their own streets, not out toward you.

The approach to {x} is blocked by a hasty checkpoint: overturned carts, armed men who are not the regular watch, a hard question about your business before you are allowed within sight of the gate. Whatever is happening inside, they have decided strangers are a risk.

{x} is quiet in the way a held breath is quiet. The slave market at its heart (you can see the empty auction platform from the gate) stands deserted, ringed by guards. The chains are still there. The people who wore them are not.

There are bodies being carried through {x}'s streets under cloth, and the people carrying them are not mourners but labourers doing grim, fast work. The rising that did this is not finished; you can hear it, somewhere in the lower districts, still going on.
The manacle-maker's shop in {x} is shuttered and scorched: the only burned building on the street, which tells you the fire was a statement, not an accident.
{x}'s field gangs work without overseers today, or the overseers have dressed like the gangs. From the road you cannot tell which, and that is the whole story of the settlement this season.
{x} and {x} maintain a relationship that exists in legal grey territory. {x} provides legitimate cover, {x} ensures market access that official channels wouldn't permit.
The books of {x} are clean because {x} keeps certain entries off them; the arrangement benefits both parties and would survive scrutiny by neither.
What {x} sells is respectability, and {x} is a steady customer. Goods move through channels no inspector has thought to draw on a map.
If either is investigated, the other is implicated. Both know this. Neither mentions it.
A clerk has begun cross-referencing the ledgers. Neither party has decided what to do about it.
One profitable season more, {x} keeps saying. The seasons keep being profitable.
{x}'s operation charges {x} a "security fee" that is, in practice, a protection racket. {x} pays without complaint because the alternative is worse.
Every month {x} pays {x} for protection against dangers that would, on inspection, trace back to {x}. Both sides account for it as a cost of doing business.
The "security fee" {x} collects from {x} buys exactly one thing: the absence of {x}. It is paid punctually.
{x} is quietly documenting every payment. Someone is being prepared for a fall.
The fee went up this quarter without explanation. {x}'s patience is a finite ledger.
A rival crew has offered {x} a better rate. Accepting would be a declaration of war on {x}.
{x} receives regular payments from {x}'s organization in exchange for patrol schedules and advance notice of raids. Both maintain professional courtesy in public.
{x}'s operation runs on a schedule {x} provides: patrols that turn a street early, raids announced a day in advance. In public the two exchange formal nods.
{x}'s clearance record looks respectable because {x} decides which crimes get cleared. The price of the arrangement is itemised and paid on time.
A new superior has started asking uncomfortable questions about clearance rates. One of them will have to act before the other does.
An honest sergeant has been transferred into {x}'s command. Both parties consider this a problem.
The payments have started arriving late. In this trade, late is a message.
{x} has made dismantling {x}'s operation a personal priority. The feeling is mutual.
{x} keeps a file on {x}'s operation that grows by the week; {x} keeps one on {x} that is already complete.
The war between {x} and {x} is fought in raids, informants, and paperwork. Neither side counts it as winnable; neither will stop.
{x} has leverage on someone close to {x}. It hasn't been used yet.
{x} is one warrant away from a raid that would end it. The warrant keeps not being signed.
Someone in {x}'s command reports to {x}. The file says so; it does not say who.
{x}'s company is retained by {x}'s interests on an exclusive basis. The arrangement works well enough that official channels have stopped asking questions.
{x} pays {x}'s company well and exclusively, and in return certain cargoes move unescorted and uninspected. The arrangement predates every official who might question it.
The contract between {x} and {x} is renewed annually with a handshake; what it actually covers has never been written down anywhere.
The contract is up for renewal. {x} has been approached by a competitor. {x} doesn't know yet.
{x}'s men have started asking what exactly they are guarding. {x} prefers them incurious.
The last shipment was short, and each side privately blames the other. The next one will settle the question.
{x} and {x} operate as a unified authority: temporal and spiritual power reinforcing each other. Dissent against one is dissent against both.
Between {x}'s pulpit and {x}'s garrison, the settlement is governed twice over; the sermons and the patrol routes have a way of agreeing.
{x} blesses what {x} enforces, and {x} enforces what {x} blesses. Where one authority ends and the other begins is a question neither permits.
They disagree on a fundamental question of method that neither will put into writing.
A penitent has brought a case that pits doctrine against order. It has not been resolved. It will not stay private.
The crowd that obeys them both has begun to notice it is one crowd. So has {x}.
{x}'s religious position provides {x}'s operation with legitimacy, meeting spaces, and an excuse for financial flows that would otherwise attract scrutiny.
{x}'s money passes through {x}'s offertory and comes out consecrated; the meeting rooms are sanctified, the accounts are not examined.
{x} provides the sanctity, {x} provides the income, and the congregation provides the cover (unknowingly), which is what makes it work.
{x} has a genuine crisis of conscience that {x} is not prepared to accommodate.
A visiting cleric has asked to audit the shrine's books. {x} has offered to handle it.
{x} has started keeping a second set of records. Confession, of a kind.
{x} provides {x}'s network with components, identification services, and the occasional forged document that only a skilled practitioner could produce.

The war reaches {x} as a series of demands rather than battles: levies of men, of {x}, of coin, each one framed as duty and none of them refusable. {x} is losing people and resources it will not get back, and the front it is bleeding for is somewhere it will never see.

The new faith has taken the young of {x} first, which the old faith has noticed and cannot answer. You cannot argue a congregation back, and every festival now draws two crowds of visibly different ages to two different squares.
{x} in {x} backed the winning faith a little too early and a little too visibly, and now find that a matter of belief has become a matter of who owes whom: the worst kind of debt to have taken on.

The conversion in {x} is being managed as a property question as much as a spiritual one: which endowments, which burial rights, which festival days transfer with the congregation. The theology was settled quickly. The estate is where the fighting is.

The revolt in {x} is past the point where it could be resolved by show of force alone. The enslaved population controls enough territory and has enough organisation that suppression would require commitment the governing faction has not yet made. The market infrastructure that generated this situation is suspended. The question now is what the settlement looks like on the other side, and who decides.

{x} has stopped functioning as the thing it was. The labour it was built on has withdrawn itself, by force, and every calculation the settlement made about its own wealth turns out to have rested on people who are no longer willing to be a line in the ledger.

The rising in {x} did not come from nowhere, though {x} is speaking of it as though it did. Everyone who is honest knows the grievances were real, old, and ignored, which makes the question of how to end it far harder than the question of how it began.

In {x} the two sides have discovered they cannot simply win: the enslaved cannot hold the whole settlement, and {x} cannot retake it without destroying the {x} that made it worth holding. Everything before the {x} is referred to as 'the old settlement'. What exists now was built after, by different people, with different assumptions, over different rubble

The {x} is why the relationship between civic and religious authority here is more carefully managed than in settlements that have never had to think about it
The {x} is the reason this settlement is here at all, in its current form, not because it was founded then, but because it was remade then, and what was remade is what we have
The people here carry the {x} the way other places carry a founding myth, except this one is remembered accurately, by people who were there, which makes it a heavier thing to live beside

A settlement with enough history that the layers show. The {x} left a foundation; everything built on top of it shows the seams
Old enough to have contradicted itself. The {x} established one set of assumptions; subsequent events revised them, not always cleanly

Several significant events, no single defining one. The character formed through accumulation rather than rupture, which makes it harder to explain and more durable

Unremarkable in its history, which is itself a kind of distinction: no catastrophe, no conquest, no great disruption. It simply continued, which required more work than it looks

The kind of place that historians overlook and travellers remember fondly: no dramatic history, but a persistent one
Stable enough that its tensions are the slow kind: inherited grievances, unresolved inheritances, debts that have been rolled over so many times no one remembers the original amount
A settlement shaped by the accumulated weight of {x} and {x}: no single defining moment, but enough of them that the character formed anyway
Shaped by events that left no monuments but changed things nonetheless: the kind of history that only becomes visible in the way people behave
A settlement that has built its identity around commerce rather than conflict. The {x} proved that economic power endures longer than military prestige

The {x} divided this settlement's relationship to faith in ways that never fully healed: the institution persisted; the unity didn't

The {x} is why the local clergy and the civic authority maintain a relationship of careful, documented mutual respect rather than the easy cooperation you find elsewhere
Visitors sometimes ask why the people here seem so personally invested in theological questions that most settlements leave to the priests. The {x} is the explanation

The {x} is why this settlement treats arcane matters with more caution than neighbours do, not superstition, institutional memory

The settlement relies on arcane workings it does not entirely trust. The {x} proved the two feelings can coexist indefinitely, and here they do, in the same shrug people give the weather

In {x} the older residents and the younger ones are not arguing about the same things. The older generation thinks the argument is about values; the younger thinks it is about access. Both are right.
{x} carries the memory of an occupation that officially ended. Collaborators and resisters still share the same streets, the same market, the same {x}. The official position is that this is resolved.

A land dispute in {x} that was dormant is now active. Someone filed a claim, or found a document, or simply started pressing. {x} has delayed ruling because there is no outcome that does not cost them something.

{x} is absorbing people it did not plan for, or losing people it expected to keep. Either way, the settlement's social assumptions no longer match its actual composition, and {x} is governing for the settlement that used to exist.
{x} has not had a strong authority since {x} left or died. The pretense of normal governance is maintained. Every decision of consequence is being deferred or made informally by {x}.
the faction with the most to gain
The most important thing happening in {x} right now is happening below the surface: {x} knows it and isn't discussing it.
Emergency committee with authority over rationing, conscription, and defence spending; not accountable to normal governance.
Under occupation, several noble families have made private accommodations with the new authority. Others have not, and are watched.
External administrative body; all significant decisions require approval or reversal. Locally hated. Their actual power depends on how many soldiers they have here, which varies.
Distributed cells operating through existing social structures; no formal hierarchy. Currently cautious.
Noble houses backing the current crown line; their support is conditional on continued royal favour and land grants.
Claims legitimate authority through different means; controls a distinct district or institution.
Noble houses that want a renegotiation of feudal obligations; not openly rebellious, but not cooperative.
Would support stability, if a price can be agreed. Currently being courted by both sides.
A coalition of noble houses that hold the crown's debt. They are owed money, military obligations, and political appointments. They are in no hurry to be repaid.
Resident agent of the external creditor; formally an observer, in practice a veto on fiscal decisions.
Several of these houses hold crown debt and are positioning accordingly.
Informal coalition demanding answers; politically inconvenient to governance; growing.
An external interest with embedded assets in at least two factions. Its presence is not known to the settlement.
The succession crisis has transformed latent noble power into active leverage. Every claimant needs their backing.
A noble house with a plausible hereditary claim; controls several key military levies. Legally strongest. Not universally liked.
Hereditary or institutional claim; has legal arguments; lacks popular support.
A rival noble house backed by popular sentiment and merchant capital; weaker bloodline claim but stronger coalition. Moving fast.
Popular support; questionable legitimacy; moving fast.
Whoever controls the remaining food reserves holds more real power than any formal authority.
Healers, clerics, and pragmatists with emergency health powers. Unpopular. Probably right.
Outside professionals brought in or passing through; temporarily powerful because they are useful.
Currently under pressure from both sides to publicly endorse the legitimate authority.
Organised common-population movement challenging the governing authority's legitimacy. Growing quickly. No unified leadership yet, which makes negotiation impossible.
Elite faction that has concluded the current governing arrangement is no longer viable. Pursuing institutional change through strategic non-cooperation, coalition-building, and selective pressure.

The incoming population has begun self-organising. Informal leadership, mutual aid networks, collective negotiation with landlords and employers. Not yet a formal political force, but cohesive enough to matter.
The institution's charitable work among new arrivals has dramatically expanded its community standing.
The arrival of skilled workers outside guild structures is an existential concern being discussed at every chapter meeting.
Informal group coordinating group departures, selling assets, and managing the logistics of relocation. Their existence is a public statement about the settlement's prospects.
Managing the emigration crisis while maintaining the appearance that it is not a crisis.
Wartime has transformed this faction from a civic institution into a primary power centre. Crown authority flows through military channels now.
War contracts have made the well-connected wealthy. The faction is divided between those profiting and those whose trade routes are severed.
Trade disruption and requisition are hurting the bottom line. The faction is lobbying for compensation and receiving promises.
The pastoral burden of wartime (soldiers praying before departure, families grieving) has made the institution indispensable in a way it wasn't before.
Crown-appointed emergency body coordinating supply, conscription, and military contracting. Currently functioning smoothly: the war is going well enough that its authority isn't contested.
Crown-appointed emergency body with powers over requisition, conscription, and price controls. Unpopular. Accused of favouritism in contract awards. Probably correct on the military decisions.
Merchants, clergy, and common voices arguing that the cost of continued war exceeds any achievable gain. Not traitors: pragmatists. Growing.
Losing congregation to the new faith faster than leadership acknowledges publicly.
One of two competing factions claiming the legitimate succession: legal standing of their records is contested.
Formally compliant with the conversion order. Actual compliance among the congregation is harder to assess.
Under pressure from both religious factions to make a formal declaration of support. Has so far avoided doing so.
Growing movement without formal institutions. Meeting in homes, sharing resources, organising mutual aid. Politically naive but numerically significant and increasingly confident.
The breakaway faction in the religious schism. Claims doctrinal legitimacy and holds parallel services. Legal standing of its records and sacraments is disputed by the established institution.
External or crown-appointed body with authority to verify compliance with the conversion order. Uses informants. Its definition of compliance is stricter than the governing faction anticipated.

Not officially a faction: officially it doesn't exist. In practice it is the most cohesive social network in the settlement. Its membership overlaps with several other factions in ways nobody discusses.
Managing an active slave revolt: the public posture is control, the private reality is containment at best.
Fully deployed for containment. Soldiers are being asked to do things that will complicate their relationship with the civilian population.

The revolt has disrupted labour supply and market operations. The faction is divided between those demanding immediate suppression and those quietly calculating whether a negotiated settlement might be cheaper.
Under pressure from both sides to publicly declare the revolt either just or sacrilegious. Has so far avoided a direct statement.
Organised leadership of the enslaved population: distributed, resilient, and holding territory. Has demands. Has not yet committed to whether those demands are negotiable.
Free citizens, clergy, and outside agitators who have been supporting the revolt covertly: shelter, information, supplies. Their involvement is not yet public.

The watch is too thinly spread to maintain order.

Petty theft, minor fraud, and opportunistic violence are persistent. No single dominant organisation: just the steady pressure of too many people with too little, and too few consequences for taking.{x}
Hunger-driven theft of food, livestock, and stored goods. Enforcement struggles to distinguish survival crime from organised theft.
Controlled goods (grain, salt, preserved meat) changing hands at extortionate prices through unofficial channels.
Sabotage, information-passing, and low-level violence against occupation infrastructure. Officially classified as criminal; morally contested.
Residents profiting by informing on neighbours or manipulating occupation administration. Source of deep social tension.
Movement restrictions ignored for economic necessity or family access. Creates both genuine public health risk and enforcement revenue.
Price gouging on medicines, protective herbs, and burial services. Often conducted by otherwise respectable merchants.
Residents fleeing creditor obligations, transferring assets fraudulently, or using criminal networks to avoid collection.
Street-level confrontations between insurgent supporters and the watch. Officially categorised as riot and disorder.
Targeted intimidation and occasional violence against officials loyal to the current authority. Professionally executed.
Both the governing faction and the insurgency pressure individuals to declare allegiance. Refusal is dangerous. False declarations are common.
Intelligence about the other side commands real money. Both factions pay for names, plans, and movements.
Active armed conflict between revolt participants and security forces in contested districts. Civilians are avoiding specific streets. The watch has abandoned normal patrol patterns.
Organised infrastructure helping enslaved persons escape. Safe houses, forged papers, passage out of the settlement. The same network that was small and cautious is now large and urgent.
Both the authorities and the revolt leadership are pressing people for information. Silence is being interpreted as allegiance. Some residents have left rather than be forced to choose.
Stolen and improvised weapons circulating in the revolt-held districts. Some are being smuggled in from outside. The black market is very active.
Banned or contested religious practice continuing in private homes, cellars, and outbuildings. Informal networks providing space, materials, and warning of enforcement activity.
False conversion declarations sold or arranged for a fee. Forged certification of compliance. Priests accepting payment to record conversions that did not occur.
Religious buildings, land, and endowments whose ownership is legally ambiguous following the change in religious authority. Being occupied, transferred, or stripped by whoever moves fastest.
Enforcement authorities paying for information about non-compliant households. Neighbour reporting on neighbour. Some reports are sincere. Many are settled scores.
Suppliers adulterating grain and leather sold to crown contracts. Inspectors are overworked or bribed. The settlement's reputation for reliable supply is being consumed for short-term profit.
Deserters passing through require food, forged papers, and discretion. A small industry has emerged to provide all three. Officially classified as harbouring criminals.
Wealthy families paying poorer ones to send sons in their place. The practice is illegal, widespread, and poorly enforced. It concentrates the actual dying in specific households.
Theft and petty fraud by new arrivals with no local ties and no established credit. The watch struggles to distinguish transients from residents.
Violent incidents between established residents and newcomers. Usually starts with an economic dispute and escalates.
Forged residence documents, unofficial lodging, underground routes for those authorities have turned away. Very profitable.

A modest shadow economy (~{x}% of activity) operates alongside legitimate commerce. Noticeable but not yet structurally damaging.
A local family wants evidence of tax extortion gathered quietly, but the extorter wears an official badge.

A guild merchant hired the party, then asked them to do something the guild officially forbids. The job was lucrative. The question is who else knows.

The garrison chaplain and the commander are the same man. He's authorizing military action for reasons that sound theological.
The merchant guild's private security force just detained someone, with no legal authority to do so. The watch is looking the other way.
